name: Vesuvius & the burial of Pompeii
scope: The volcano over the Bay of Naples that buried two Roman towns in a single afternoon in AD 79. T1: Mount Vesuvius rises behind Naples in southern Italy; in AD 79 it buried the town of Pompeii under meters of ash and pumice, freezing a whole Roman city in time. T2: the people of Pompeii were not killed by lava but by a pyroclastic surge -- a ~300C avalanche of superheated gas and ash that killed instantly. T3: a young man, Pliny the Younger, watched from Misenum across the bay and wrote the only eyewitness account, comparing the eruption cloud to an umbrella-pine tree -- which is why this towering-column eruption style is now called 'Plinian.' T4: his uncle, Pliny the Elder, sailed the Roman fleet TOWARD the eruption to rescue friends and died on the beach at Stabiae. T5: the famous body 'casts' of Pompeii are plaster -- archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli poured plaster into the hollow VOIDS left in the hardened ash where victims' bodies had decayed. Deeper rungs: nearby Herculaneum was buried by hotter flows that CARBONIZED a whole library of papyrus scrolls (the Villa of the Papyri), now being read unopened by X-ray scanning and AI (the Vesuvius Challenge); Vesuvius is a 'somma' volcano, a young cone growing inside the ring of an older collapsed crater; and ~3 million people now live in its shadow.
source: Wikipedia: 'Eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79' (fetched/verified: Pliny the Younger's letters and 'Plinian' naming, ~300C pyroclastic surges, Fiorelli plaster casts poured into ash voids, Villa of the Papyri carbonized scrolls + Vesuvius Challenge, Pliny the Elder's death at Stabiae). Grokipedia to be checked first at build stage per policy.
framing_note: Scene-led wonder about the PLACE and the earth-process that entombed it. Accuracy rail: 'Plinian' is named for Pliny the YOUNGER (the eyewitness), NOT the Elder (who died); the casts are plaster poured into body-shaped voids, NOT petrified bodies -- keep that exact. Dinner-test payoff = the plaster casts made from body-shaped holes in the ash (T5) and the AI-read carbonized scrolls. Invert the wonder at T3 (the 'umbrella-pine cloud' is the hook; 'Plinian' is the recalled answer, not restated in the stem). Distractors are other real eruption terms (Strombolian, Vulcanian, effusive) and other buried sites (Herculaneum, Stabiae, Oplontis) so all four stay live. Lane border: geography owns the burial and the site's archaeology -- do NOT drift into the political history of Rome.
history_overlap: The AD 79 event and Pliny's account may appear in a Roman-history ladder; keep geography's answers anchored to the place and earth-process (pyroclastic burial, the plaster casts, Herculaneum's carbonized scrolls), not Roman political history.

name: Krakatoa 1883: the loudest sound on Earth
scope: The Indonesian island volcano whose 1883 eruption was the loudest event in recorded history. T1: Krakatoa (Krakatau) sat in the Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra; in 1883 it blew itself apart in an eruption heard across a quarter of the planet. T2: invert the wonder -- the final explosion was heard 4,800 km away on Rodrigues Island near Mauritius (people there thought it was distant naval cannon fire), making it the LOUDEST sound in recorded history; sailors 64 km away had their eardrums ruptured. T3: the real killer was water -- the volcano's collapse sent tsunamis over 40 m high crashing into Java and Sumatra, killing about 36,000 people. T4: the pressure wave from the blast circled the ENTIRE Earth about three and a half times, recorded on barographs worldwide for days afterward. T5: so much ash reached the high atmosphere that sunsets turned blood-red across the globe for months -- fire brigades in New York were called out to 'fires' that were only the sky. Deeper: a new island, Anak Krakatau ('Child of Krakatoa'), rose from the same submarine crater in the late 1920s, and its flank collapse triggered a deadly tsunami in 2018.
source: Wikipedia: '1883 eruption of Krakatoa' (fetched/verified: sound heard 4,800 km at Rodrigues Island, official death toll 36,417 mostly from tsunami, tsunami up to ~40+ m, pressure wave circled globe ~3.5 times, worldwide blood-red sunsets, Anak Krakatau emergence). Grokipedia to be checked first at build stage.
framing_note: Scene-led; the PLACE (Sunda Strait / Krakatoa) is the anchor and every answer is a Krakatoa fact. Invert-the-wonder is the spine (loudest sound, globe-circling pressure wave, worldwide red skies). Accuracy rail: 4,800 km / Rodrigues Island for the sound; the ~36,000 dead were mostly from the TSUNAMI, not the blast itself -- keep cause-of-death correct. Dinner-test payoff = the sound heard nearly 5,000 km away (T2) and fire engines chasing a red sky in New York (T5). Distractors are other real 'loudest/biggest' claims and adjacent eruptions (Tambora, Pinatubo, Mount Pelee) so all four stay live. Any Munch 'The Scream' red-sky link is a labeled hypothesis, not a fact.

name: Tambora & the Year Without a Summer
scope: The 1815 Indonesian eruption so vast it changed the world's weather for a year. T2: Mount Tambora on the island of Sumbawa, Indonesia, erupted in 1815 in the most powerful eruption in recorded history (VEI 7), blasting away the top third of the mountain and killing about 71,000 people. T3: invert the wonder -- the following year, 1816, became known worldwide as 'the Year Without a Summer': snow fell in New England in June and harvests failed across Europe and North America, all traced back to Tambora's dust. T4: trapped indoors by the gloomy, storm-dark summer of 1816 beside Lake Geneva, 18-year-old Mary Shelley began writing 'Frankenstein' -- a novel born from a volcanic winter half a world away. T5: the mechanism is the deep wonder -- Tambora flung sulfur gas high into the STRATOSPHERE, where it formed a haze of sulfate-droplet aerosols that reflected sunlight back to space and cooled the whole planet for over a year.
source: Wikipedia: '1815 eruption of Mount Tambora' (fetched/verified: VEI 7, most powerful eruption in recorded history, Sumbawa, ~71,000 deaths, 1816 Year Without a Summer with June frosts/snow in New England, Turner's altered skies). Mary Shelley / Villa Diodati summer 1816 is widely documented. Grokipedia to be checked first at build.
framing_note: Earth-process wonder anchored to Sumbawa; the answer is always a Tambora/1816 fact. Accuracy rail: Tambora 1815 is the LARGEST eruption in recorded history (bigger than Krakatoa); the cooling worked via sulfate aerosols in the stratosphere reflecting sunlight -- state the mechanism plainly, no climate alarmism. Dinner-test payoff = 'the Year Without a Summer' (T3) and Frankenstein born from it (T4). Distractors are other real eruptions and other historically cold years so all four stay live. Lane border: the novel is a one-rung cultural payoff BORN of the place's climate effect, not a literature ladder.

name: Pinatubo 1991: the eruption that cooled the planet
scope: The Philippine volcano whose 1991 eruption measurably cooled the whole Earth -- and whose forecast saved tens of thousands of lives. T2: Mount Pinatubo, on the island of Luzon in the Philippines, roared back to life in 1991 after about 500 years of silence, in the second-largest eruption of the 20th century. T3: invert the wonder -- it injected about 17 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere, and over the next two years global temperatures dropped by roughly half a degree Celsius -- a whole planet cooled by one mountain. T4: scientists from the Philippine institute PHIVOLCS and the U.S. Geological Survey read the warning signs and ordered a mass evacuation days before the blast, saving tens of thousands of lives; the giant U.S. Clark Air Base nearby was abandoned. T5: teach the term 'lahar' -- the danger did not end with the eruption; for years afterward, monsoon rains remobilized the loose ash into lahars, fast rivers of volcanic mud that buried whole towns downstream.
source: Wikipedia: '1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo' (fetched/verified: global cooling ~0.4C / NH ~0.5-0.6C for ~1991-93, ~17 Mt SO2 largest ever measured, second-largest 20th-century eruption after Novarupta 1912, VEI 6, ~60,000 evacuated saving tens of thousands, Clark Air Base abandoned, multi-year lahars). Grokipedia first at build.
framing_note: Earth-process + human-preparedness wonder anchored to Luzon. Accuracy rail: ~0.5C global cooling and ~17 Mt SO2 (the largest sulfur injection ever measured by instruments); the successful evacuation is the humane payoff -- credit PHIVOLCS + USGS honestly. Dinner-test payoff = 'one mountain cooled the whole planet half a degree' (T3). Teach 'lahar' via the T5 scene before naming it. Distractors are other real eruptions and other climate effects (the ozone hole, El Nino) so all four stay live. No alarmism -- settled earth science told with wonder.

name: Laki 1783: the fissure that starved a nation
scope: Not a cone but a CRACK in Iceland that bled lava for eight months and caused a famine. T2: in 1783 the ground tore open along a 25-km fissure in southern Iceland called Lakagigar ('the craters of Laki'), and lava poured from a row of more than 130 vents -- a 'fissure eruption,' not a single mountain. T3: invert the wonder -- the eruption's gas, not its lava, was the killer: clouds of fluorine settled on the grass and poisoned Iceland's livestock (about 80% of the sheep died of it), and the famine that followed, the Modhardhindin or 'Mist Hardships,' killed roughly a fifth of everyone in Iceland. T4: the bluish sulfur haze drifted across Europe that summer -- in America, Benjamin Franklin noted a strange 'dry fog' that dimmed the sun -- and the crop failures it caused killed tens of thousands more (about 23,000 in Britain alone). T5: some historians argue that the misery Laki spread across France helped stoke the unrest that led toward the French Revolution six years later (a genuinely debated link).
source: Wikipedia: 'Laki' (fetched/verified: 25-km fissure, 130+ vents, ~20-25% of Iceland's population died from famine, ~80% of sheep dead from fluorosis, Modhardhindin 'Mist Hardships', ~8 Mt fluorine and ~120 Mt SO2, ~23,000 British deaths, Franklin's 'dry fog'). Grokipedia first at build.
framing_note: Earth-process wonder anchored to Iceland; teach 'fissure eruption' via the scene (a 25-km crack, a row of 130 vents) rather than defining it cold. Accuracy rail: the mass deaths were from FLUORINE-poisoned livestock and the resulting famine, not from lava burning people -- keep cause correct; ~20% of Iceland's population. Dinner-test payoff = a crack in the ground, not a mountain, starved a whole country (T3). The French Revolution link is flagged as a DEBATED hypothesis, never stated as fact. Distractors are other Icelandic volcanoes and other eruption styles so all four stay live.

name: Mount St Helens 1980: the sideways blast
scope: The Washington State volcano that erupted SIDEWAYS. T1: Mount St Helens, a snow-capped cone in Washington State, USA, erupted on 18 May 1980 in the deadliest and most destructive eruption in United States history. T2: for weeks beforehand a huge 'bulge' swelled out of the mountain's north face, growing about 1.5 m per DAY as magma pushed underneath. T3: invert the wonder -- a morning earthquake shook the bulge loose in the LARGEST landslide in recorded history, and that avalanche uncorked the magma so the volcano exploded not upward but SIDEWAYS, a lateral blast that flattened forest across nearly 600 sq km. T4: geologist David Johnston, camped 10 km north, radioed 'Vancouver! Vancouver! This is it!' seconds before the blast reached him; 57 people died, including innkeeper Harry Truman, who had refused to leave his lodge on the mountain. T5: the mountain lost about 400 m of its summit in minutes (from 2,950 m down to about 2,550 m), leaving a mile-wide horseshoe crater where the peak had stood. Deeper: nearby Spirit Lake was buried under a raft of shattered logs that still floats on it today, and a new lava dome has slowly rebuilt inside the crater ever since.
source: Wikipedia: '1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens' (fetched/verified: 18 May 1980, M5.1 quake triggering the largest subaerial landslide in recorded history, the lateral blast, bulge growth ~5-6 ft/day, 57 dead, summit 9,677 ft -> 8,363 ft, ~230 sq mi of flattened forest). David Johnston's final radio call is documented. Grokipedia first at build.
framing_note: Scene-led drama anchored to the named mountain; every answer is a St Helens fact. Accuracy rail: the LATERAL (sideways) blast and the record landslide are the twin wonders -- keep the sequence right (quake -> record landslide -> uncorked lateral blast); 57 dead. Dinner-test payoff = a volcano that blew out sideways (T3) and Johnston's last radio call (T4). Distractors are other eruption styles and other Cascade volcanoes (Rainier, Hood, Shasta) so all four stay live.

name: The Hawaiian hotspot & the island conveyor belt
scope: One fixed plume of magma under the Pacific has built an entire chain of islands as the seafloor drifts over it. T1: the Hawaiian Islands sit in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, nowhere near a plate edge, yet Kilauea and Mauna Loa on the Big Island are among the most active volcanoes on Earth. T2: the wonder is a 'hotspot' -- a fixed plume of hot rock rising from deep in the mantle; as the Pacific Plate slides slowly northwest over it (about 7-10 cm a year), the plume punches out a new volcano, then that island drifts off the hotspot and the next one begins -- a conveyor belt of islands. T3: on a fresh Kilauea flow you can see two lava textures side by side -- smooth, silvery, ropy sheets and sharp clinkery rubble; Hawaiians gave the smooth kind the name 'pahoehoe' and the jagged kind 'aa', both now used by scientists worldwide. T4: invert the wonder -- measured from its base on the deep ocean floor, Mauna Kea rises about 10,000 m, making it the TALLEST mountain on Earth from base to summit, taller than Everest, though most of it is underwater. T5: the chain doesn't stop at Hawaii -- it continues as a line of drowned 'seamounts' for about 6,000 km, and where the trail bends sharply (about 120 degrees) the rocks record that the whole Pacific Plate changed direction roughly 47-50 million years ago. Deeper: the NEXT Hawaiian island, Kamaehuakanaloa (formerly Loihi), is already growing as a seamount off the Big Island's coast, still deep underwater.
source: Wikipedia: 'Hawaiian-Emperor seamount chain' (fetched/verified: ~120-degree bend formed ~47-50 Ma, chain ~6,200 km, Kamaehuakanaloa/Loihi the youngest) and 'Mauna Kea' (fetched/verified: ~9,966 m from its base in the Hawaiian Trough, tallest base-to-summit, measurement-dependent). Grokipedia first at build.
framing_note: EARTH-SYSTEM ladder: the spine is the HOTSPOT process, deepened across named Hawaiian places (Kilauea, Mauna Kea, the seamount chain, Kamaehuakanaloa). Every rung names a place; the answer is a place/earth-process fact. Teach 'hotspot,' 'pahoehoe/aa,' and 'seamount' via scene, not cold definition. Accuracy rail: Mauna Kea is tallest FROM ITS BASE (measurement-dependent, taller than Everest base-to-peak) -- say 'from its base,' NOT 'highest above sea level'; the bend records a plate-motion change ~47-50 Ma, and the ANGLE is ~120 degrees (47 is the age, not the angle). Dinner-test payoff = the tallest-mountain-from-its-base reveal (T4) and the pahoehoe/aa lava names (T3). Distractors: other Pacific volcanoes and other superlatives (highest above sea level, most massive -- Mauna Loa) so all four stay live. Lane border: Hawaii's wildlife is the ANIMAL bank; geography owns the volcanic landscape.

name: Yellowstone: the supervolcano under the park
scope: America's first national park sits inside the crater of a sleeping supervolcano. T1: Yellowstone in Wyoming, USA, is famous for its geysers and rainbow-colored hot springs -- and the whole park sits on top of one of the world's largest volcanic systems. T2: invert the wonder -- the reason for all the geysers, the vast Grand Prismatic Spring, and Old Faithful is a giant chamber of molten rock a few kilometers down heating the groundwater; Yellowstone holds about HALF of all the geysers on Earth. T3: teach the term -- the park sits inside a 'caldera,' a basin roughly 55 by 72 km wide that formed when the ground collapsed into an emptied magma chamber after a colossal eruption. T4: Yellowstone has had three giant eruptions; the most recent, the Lava Creek event about 640,000 years ago, ejected around 1,000 cubic km of rock -- a 'supervolcano' eruption thousands of times larger than Mount St Helens. T5: the hotspot itself hasn't moved -- the North American Plate has DRIFTED southwest over it, leaving a 700-km trail of older calderas across the Snake River Plain of Idaho, like a scorch mark showing where the continent has slid.
source: Wikipedia: 'Yellowstone Caldera' (fetched/verified: Lava Creek Tuff ~640,000 ya ~1,000 cubic km, Huckleberry Ridge ~2.08 Ma ~2,450 cubic km, Snake River Plain hotspot track). Caldera ~55x72 km and 'about half the world's geysers' are standard USGS/NPS figures. Grokipedia first at build.
framing_note: Keystone place-ladder with the hotspot earth-process as its spine. Accuracy rail: teach 'caldera' before testing it; last supereruption ~640,000 years ago (Lava Creek) -- do NOT imply it is 'overdue' or frame it as alarm; the hotspot is fixed and the PLATE moved (same physics as Hawaii). Dinner-test payoff = the geysers are the surface sign of a supervolcano's magma (T2) and the Snake River Plain 'scorch mark' trail (T5). Distractors: other calderas/supervolcanoes (Long Valley, Toba, Campi Flegrei) and other geyser fields (Iceland, New Zealand) so all four stay live.

name: Etna, Stromboli & the word 'volcano'
scope: The Mediterranean volcanoes the ancient Romans watched -- one of them gave us the very word 'volcano.' T1: Mount Etna towers over eastern Sicily, Italy -- the largest and most active volcano in Europe, erupting so often that its lava flows and ash clouds are an ordinary part of Sicilian life. T2: just north lies little Stromboli, which has erupted almost continuously for THOUSANDS of years, tossing up glowing bursts of lava every few minutes; sailors have used its red glow as a natural beacon and call it the 'Lighthouse of the Mediterranean.' T3: teach the term -- those brief, rhythmic bursts of incandescent lava blobs are so characteristic of Stromboli that this whole eruption style is named after it: 'Strombolian.' T4: invert the wonder -- nearby is a small island the Romans called Vulcano, believing it was the smoking chimney of Vulcan, their god of the forge; from that one island's name comes the English word 'volcano.' T5: the ancient Greeks explained Etna differently -- they said the monster Typhon (or the smith-god Hephaestus's forge) lay pinned beneath the mountain, its struggles shaking the earth: a myth born to explain a real, restless place.
source: Wikipedia: 'Stromboli' (fetched/verified: near-continuous eruption ~2,000-5,000 years, 'Lighthouse of the Mediterranean', Strombolian eruption style, Aeolian Islands north of Sicily) and 'Vulcano' (island named for the god Vulcan, the etymological root of 'volcano'; standard etymology). 'Etna' as Europe's largest active volcano is well established. Grokipedia first at build.
framing_note: PLACE + etymology + myth wonder, all anchored to the named Aeolian/Sicilian volcanoes. Accuracy rail: the 'Lighthouse of the Mediterranean' is STROMBOLI (not Etna); 'volcano' comes from the island Vulcano / the god Vulcan -- keep that etymology exact. Dinner-test payoff = the word 'volcano' itself comes from a real Italian island (T4). The Typhon/Hephaestus story is labeled as ancient myth that explains the place, not fact. Distractors: other eruption styles (Plinian, Vulcanian, Hawaiian) and other Italian volcanoes (Vesuvius, Vulcano, Vulture) so all four stay live.

name: Iceland: where two continents pull apart
scope: A whole country built on the seam where two continents are tearing apart. T1: Iceland, in the north Atlantic, is a land of fire and ice -- glaciers sit right on top of active volcanoes, and one island holds more than 30 active volcanic systems. T2: the reason is that Iceland straddles the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the underwater mountain seam where the North American and Eurasian plates pull APART; Iceland is the rare place where that rift rises above the sea, so the country is literally splitting -- about 2 cm wider every year. T3: at Thingvellir you can walk down into the rift valley between the two plates, in the Almannagja gorge, and stand with North America on one wall and Europe on the other. T4: invert the wonder -- in 2010 a volcano under the Eyjafjallajokull glacier erupted through ice, and its fine ash cloud grounded European air travel for days, cancelling roughly 100,000 flights and stranding millions -- an eruption that shut down a continent's skies. T5: in 1973 on the island of Heimaey, townspeople fought back against an advancing lava flow that was closing off their harbor -- pumping millions of tonnes of seawater onto the lava to cool and stop it, and they SAVED the harbor. Deeper: floods called jokulhlaups burst out when a volcano melts a glacier from beneath (Grimsvotn under Vatnajokull), and the recent Fagradalsfjall eruptions on the Reykjanes peninsula have drawn crowds to watch fresh lava up close.
source: Wikipedia: 'Volcanism of Iceland', 'Thingvellir' (Mid-Atlantic Ridge rift, Almannagja), 'Eyjafjallajokull' + '2010 eruptions of Eyjafjallajokull' (~100,000 flights cancelled), 'Eldfell' (1973 Heimaey seawater lava-cooling that saved the harbor), 'Jokulhlaup'/'Grimsvotn'. Grokipedia first at build.
framing_note: EARTH-SYSTEM ladder: the spine is the DIVERGENT plate boundary (the Mid-Atlantic Ridge on land), deepened across named Icelandic places. Teach 'Mid-Atlantic Ridge,' 'rift,' 'jokulhlaup' via scene. Accuracy rail: Iceland sits on the ridge AND a hotspot (both true); the plates DIVERGE (pull apart) here -- never say they collide. Dinner-test payoff = standing in the crack between two continents at Thingvellir (T3) and hosing lava with seawater to save Heimaey's harbor (T5). Distractors: other plate boundaries and other Icelandic volcanoes so all four stay live. Lane border: Thingvellir's Althing parliament is a one-clause history/culture aside -- the ANSWER is the plate-boundary rift, not the parliament.
history_overlap: Thingvellir's Althing (one of the world's oldest parliaments, founded 930 AD) may appear in a history/culture ladder -- keep this ladder's answer the geological rift, not the parliament's founding.

name: Santorini: the caldera behind the Atlantis legend
scope: A crescent-shaped Greek island that is really the rim of a drowned volcano. T2: Santorini (ancient Thera) in the Aegean Sea is a ring of steep cliffs curving around a deep blue bay -- the whole island is the wall of a 'caldera,' the flooded crater left when a volcano collapsed into the sea. T3: around 1600 BC Thera erupted in one of the largest eruptions in human history (VEI 7); the center of the island collapsed, letting the sea rush in and forming the crescent shape visitors sail into today. T4: invert the wonder -- buried under the ash at Akrotiri lies a Bronze Age town so well preserved it's called the 'Minoan Pompeii,' with three-story houses and vivid frescoes -- but UNLIKE Pompeii, almost NO bodies have been found, so the townspeople seem to have fled in time. T5: because the eruption devastated the nearby Minoan civilization on Crete, some scholars have proposed Thera as the real place behind Plato's legend of Atlantis, the great island that vanished into the sea (a popular idea, but not accepted by most scholars).
source: Wikipedia: 'Minoan eruption' (fetched/verified: ~1600 BC eruption, ice-core ~1628 BC and disputed dating, VEI 7, caldera collapse forming the crescent island, Akrotiri the 'Minoan Pompeii' with no human remains found, Marinatos's Atlantis hypothesis NOT supported by current scholarship). Grokipedia first at build.
framing_note: PLACE-wonder anchored to Santorini/Thera; every answer is a Santorini fact. Teach 'caldera' via the scene (the cliff ring around a drowned crater). Accuracy rail: the Atlantis link is a labeled HYPOTHESIS (proposed by Marinatos, not supported by current scholarship) -- never state it as fact; the eruption is ~1600 BC (ice-core ~1628 BC, disputed). Dinner-test payoff = the 'Minoan Pompeii' at Akrotiri where no bodies were found (T4). Distractors: other calderas and other Aegean/Greek islands so all four stay live. Lane border: the Minoan civilization's DECLINE is history-bank territory -- keep answers on the island's landscape and the buried town, not Bronze Age politics.
history_overlap: The Minoan civilization's collapse belongs to the history bank; keep this ladder's answers on the caldera/Akrotiri landscape and burial, not the Bronze Age political story.

name: Lava lakes: the world's eternal fire pits
scope: Only a handful of volcanoes on Earth hold a permanent, churning lake of molten lava -- here they are. T2: at Mount Nyiragongo in the Democratic Republic of Congo, a lake of liquid lava churns in the summit crater -- one of the largest lava lakes ever known, glowing above the lakeside city of Goma. T3: invert the wonder -- Nyiragongo's lava is unusually runny (very low in silica), so when its crater wall broke in 1977 the lava raced downhill at up to about 60 km/h, the fastest lava flow ever recorded -- most lava you could simply walk away from. T4: on the far side of the world, Mount Erebus in ANTARCTICA holds a lava lake too -- a pool of fire on a continent of ice, and the southernmost active volcano on Earth; and in Ethiopia's scorching Danakil Depression, Erta Ale ('the smoking mountain') has kept its lava lake for over a century. T5: strangest of all is Ol Doinyo Lengai in Tanzania, the only volcano on Earth that erupts 'natrocarbonatite' lava -- so cool (barely 500-600C) and runny that it pours out black like motor oil and then turns chalky WHITE within days; to the Maasai it is Ol Doinyo Lengai, the 'Mountain of God.'
source: Wikipedia: 'Mount Nyiragongo' (fetched/verified: most voluminous known lava lake, very low-silica lava, 1977 flow up to ~60 km/h the fastest recorded, 2002/2021 eruptions and Goma), 'Mount Erebus' (Antarctic lava lake, southernmost active volcano), 'Erta Ale' (Danakil, long-lived lava lake), 'Ol Doinyo Lengai' (unique natrocarbonatite lava ~500-590C, black cooling to white, Maasai 'Mountain of God'). Grokipedia first at build.
framing_note: EARTH-SYSTEM theme ladder: the spine is persistent LAVA LAKES and lava chemistry, deepened across named places (Nyiragongo, Erebus, Erta Ale, Ol Doinyo Lengai, with Kilauea's Halemaumau available). Every rung names a place; the answer is a place/lava fact. Accuracy rail: Nyiragongo's record speed (~60 km/h in 1977) comes from LOW-silica lava; Ol Doinyo Lengai's cool black-to-white carbonatite is genuine and unique -- keep the chemistry honest. Dinner-test payoff = the black lava that turns white / the only-in-the-world Mountain of God (T5) and a lava lake in Antarctica (T4). Respect the Maasai sacred name on its own terms -- present it plainly, neither advertise nor dismiss. Distractors: other lava-lake volcanoes and other lava types (pahoehoe, aa, basalt) so all four stay live. Lane border: geography owns the lava/landscape, not any creature living near these vents.

name: Volcanic lightning: the ash cloud's dirty thunderstorm
scope: Some eruptions crackle with their own lightning, born inside the ash instead of a rain cloud. T2: when Iceland's Eyjafjallajokull erupted in 2010, photographers caught bolts of lightning flickering INSIDE the towering ash plume -- lightning made by a volcano, with no storm at all. T3: invert the wonder -- this 'volcanic lightning' (nicknamed a 'dirty thunderstorm') comes from the ash itself: countless jagged ash particles rub and collide as they blast upward, building up static electricity until it discharges as lightning. T4: at Sakurajima in Kagoshima Bay, Japan, one of the world's most active volcanoes, these lightning storms flash so often that scientists travel there to study them; volcanic lightning also lit up the 2020 eruption of Taal in the Philippines and the 2018 collapse of Anak Krakatau. T5: it is not new -- nearly 2,000 years ago Pliny the Younger, describing Vesuvius, wrote of a darkness lit by flashes, and today satellites detect these bursts to warn aircraft that an invisible ash cloud is aloft.
source: Wikipedia: 'Volcanic lightning' (mechanism = static charge from colliding ash particles; documented at Eyjafjallajokull 2010, Sakurajima, Taal 2020, Anak Krakatau; Pliny the Younger's ancient description; satellite detection for aviation warning). Grokipedia first at build.
framing_note: EARTH-SYSTEM theme ladder: the spine is VOLCANIC LIGHTNING, deepened across named volcanoes (Eyjafjallajokull, Sakurajima, Taal, Anak Krakatau). Every rung names a place. Accuracy rail: the mechanism is STATIC charge from colliding ash particles (not ordinary weather) -- teach it via the scene at T3, keep it correct. Dinner-test payoff = lightning made inside an ash cloud with no storm (T2/T3). Distractors: other eruption/atmospheric phenomena (St Elmo's fire, pyroclastic flow, ashfall) and other volcanoes so all four stay live. The Pliny reference is a real historical description, not embroidery.

name: A volcano is born: new land in a human lifetime
scope: Sometimes people get to WATCH a brand-new mountain or island rise from nothing. T1: in 1943, in the Mexican village of Paricutin, a farmer named Dionisio Pulido watched the ground of his cornfield crack open and begin to smoke -- and a volcano was born in his field. T2: invert the wonder -- over the next nine years Paricutin grew into a 424-m cone and its lava buried the town of San Juan Parangaricutiro, leaving only the church's bell tower and altar poking up out of the hardened black lava (you can still visit them today). T3: the sea can do it too -- in 1963 fishermen off Iceland saw smoke rising from the water, and over four years a whole new island, Surtsey, rose from the waves; it is now a protected laboratory where scientists watch how life first colonizes brand-new land. T4: after Krakatoa destroyed itself in 1883, a new cone climbed from the same underwater crater in the late 1920s -- fittingly named Anak Krakatau, 'the Child of Krakatoa.' T5: it still happens today -- off Japan, undersea eruptions built and repeatedly enlarged the island of Nishinoshima through the 2010s, adding fresh territory to the map.

name: The mystery eruptions: reading Earth's ash archive
scope: Some giant eruptions marked the whole planet -- but the volcano that did it stayed a mystery for centuries. T2: ice cores drilled in Greenland and Antarctica showed that around the year 1257 SOMETHING erupted so violently it dusted BOTH poles with sulfur -- one of the biggest eruptions in 7,000 years -- yet for 750 years no one knew which volcano did it. T3: invert the wonder -- in 2013 scientists matched the ash chemistry to Mount Samalas on the island of Lombok, Indonesia; its collapse left the huge caldera that today holds the Segara Anak crater lake beside Mount Rinjani, and a medieval Javanese chronicle, the Babad Lombok, even describes a mountain that collapsed and buried a kingdom. T4: an older mystery -- in AD 536 a strange dust veil dimmed the sun for over a year across Europe and Asia (the Byzantine writer Procopius said the sun shone 'without brightness'); scientists now blame a huge volcanic eruption, though they still argue over WHERE (Iceland, or Ilopango in Central America). T5: the biggest of all is written near Lake Toba on Sumatra, Indonesia -- a caldera about 100 km long left by the largest eruption in roughly 2 million years, about 74,000 years ago; some scientists proposed it nearly wiped out early humans (the 'Toba bottleneck' -- a genuinely debated idea).

Dinner-test payoff = a giant eruption whose volcano was a mystery for 750 years, cracked by ice cores (T2/T3). Distractors: other Indonesian volcanoes and other big eruptions (Tambora, Krakatoa) so all four stay live.

name: The Door to Hell: the Darvaza gas crater
scope: A pit of fire that has burned in a desert for half a century. T1: in the Karakum Desert of Turkmenistan, a crater 60-70 m wide has been ON FIRE continuously for decades -- locals and travelers call it the 'Door to Hell' (its official name is the 'Shining of Karakum'). T2: invert the wonder -- it is NOT a volcano; it's a collapsed natural-gas field. The story goes that around 1971 Soviet drilling caused the ground to cave into a gas pocket, and engineers set the escaping methane alight expecting it to burn off in a few days -- but it has burned ever since (the exact date is uncertain; the records are classified or lost). T3: the government has tried to close it -- in 2022 the president ordered it extinguished because it wastes valuable natural gas and pollutes -- yet the fire still glows in the desert night.
